<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The `makepkg --printsrcinfo` command only sources the top-level scope of the PKGBUILD and does not execute functions such as `pkgver()`, `prepare()`, `build()`, or `package()`. In this PKGBUILD, the global scope contains only standard variable assignments: `pkgname`, `pkgver`, `pkgrel`, `pkgdesc`, `arch`, `url`, `license`, `depends`, `makedepends`, `source`, and `sha256sums`. All values are statically defined or use simple string interpolation with no command substitution.

The function `latestver()` uses `gh api` to fetch the latest release tag, but it is never called in the global scope and thus will not be executed during `makepkg --printsrcinfo`. There are no top-level commands, backticks, `$()`, or other forms of command substitution outside of functions. As such, sourcing this PKGBUILD for metadata extraction poses no risk of remote code execution, data exfiltration, or unintended network activity.

This file adheres to standard AUR packaging practices, and no malicious behavior can be triggered during the `--printsrcinfo` phase.
</details>
<evidence>

<summary>No top-level command execution; safe sourcing</summary>
</security_assessment>

<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard build and packaging process for the `psicode` package, a terminal coding agent written in C89 and Lua. The source is fetched from the official GitHub repository (siraben/psi) using a tagged release, and the SHA-256 checksum is provided and matches the expected value. There are no signs of obfuscated code, unauthorized network requests, or suspicious file operations.

The build process uses standard `make` commands with controlled environment variables for hardening and path configuration. The package renames binaries and man pages from `psi` to `psicode` to avoid conflicts with an existing package, which is a common and legitimate practice in AUR packaging. The maintainer comments explain the rationale clearly. The `check()` function runs basic verification of the built binary, which is a good hygiene practice.

No dangerous commands (e.g., `curl|bash`, `eval`, `base64` decoding, or data exfiltration attempts) are present. All operations are confined to the build and package directories, and installed files are placed in appropriate system locations. The use of `sed` to update man pages is transparent and validated with a `grep` check. The package adheres to standard AUR packaging practices and shows no evidence of malicious behavior.
</details>
